pub_hw_icecube.png: Hubel and Wiesel's ice-cube model of primary visual cortex (V1), as drawn in Kandel, Schwartz and Jessell's Principles of Neural Science. A block of cortex is shown in perspective, with cortical layers I to VI marked down its left side. The block is split into two halves, a left-eye and a right-eye ocular dominance slab. Its top surface is tiled with orientation columns, colour-coded by the legend: blue for horizontal, green for one oblique, yellow for vertical and red for the other oblique. Dashed cylinders inside each slab are the blobs. The point: one small block holds every orientation for both eyes, and the block repeats across the whole visual field.
pub_kobatake1994_rf_map.png: Kobatake and Tanaka (1994): receptive fields recorded along the macaque ventral stream. In the centre, an outline of the cortex with dots marking recording sites, from posterior on the left to anterior on the right. A line runs from each dot to the receptive field of the cells recorded there, drawn as a square or rectangle on a small cross that marks the centre of gaze. Posterior sites, on the left, connect to small squares of a few degrees close to the cross; anterior sites in inferotemporal cortex (IT), on the right, connect to large squares, the largest several times the 10-degree scale bar in the top-right corner. The point: receptive fields grow along the hierarchy.
pub_tanaka1996_table.png: Tanaka (1996): a table of example critical features, the simplest stimuli that still drove a cell, in four columns. V2, in a small box at the top left: a dark triangle and a bullseye. V4, an L-shaped region below and right of it: a starburst, a teardrop, crossed bars, framed squares, a spiky star, a disc with a small circle, a branched bar, a striped rectangle, a half-filled diamond and a thick black ring. Posterior IT: a teardrop, an X, concentric circles, a spiky star, a notched disc, a dotted bar, a striped half-disc and an ellipse in a circle. Anterior IT: a striped bar, a black blob, concentric circles, a simple face, a square with a black tab, a lollipop shape, a striped stick with a ball, a blob and a pencil shape. The point: the preferred stimulus becomes more complex from V2 to anterior IT.
pub_desimone1984_faces.png: Desimone, Albright, Gross and Bruce (1984): responses of one face-selective neuron in inferotemporal cortex. Eight spike histograms, each above the black-and-white line drawing of its stimulus, numbered 1 to 8. Stimuli 1 to 6 are versions of a monkey face: 2 has its parts cut up and rearranged, 4 and 5 have a horizontal strip of the face removed, and 6 is labelled 'no color'. Stimulus 7 is a bearded human face and 8 is a hand; a scale bar under the hand marks 2.5 degrees. The histograms are tall for the intact faces (1, 3, 5) and clearly raised for 4, 6 and 7, but low and flat for the scrambled face (2) and the hand (8). The point: the cell needs the face's parts in their arrangement.
pub_pospisil2018_apc_shapes.png: The curved shape set of Pasupathy and Connor (2001), as reproduced in Pospisil et al. (2018), Figure 1A: 51 black silhouettes in six rows. They range from a dot and a disc through ellipses, crescents and teardrops to shapes with one or more convex points and concave notches at different angular positions, ending in four-pointed stars and lobed blobs. One shape, a teardrop with a sharp point, is outlined by a red box. The point: V4 cells were tested with shapes that vary in the curvature of their boundary at each position.
tvsd_montage_4col.png: A montage of eight THINGS photographs of everyday objects from the test set of the THINGS Ventral Stream Spiking Dataset, in two rows of four, on natural or plain backgrounds.
pub_hung2005_fig1a.png: Hung, Kreiman, Poggio and DiCarlo (2005), Figure 1A. Top: five grey-background example pictures from the stimulus set, a ring-like toy shape, a vegetable, a monkey face, a cat and a car. Below each picture, spike rasters from three recording sites in inferotemporal cortex, Site 1 in blue, Site 2 in green and Site 3 in orange, with dots below for further sites. Each row of dots is one presentation; each dot is a spike. A black bar under each column and the label '0 100 ms' give the time scale. The point: each site fires differently for different pictures within about 100 ms.
pub_hung2005_fig1b.png: Hung, Kreiman, Poggio and DiCarlo (2005), Figure 1B: classification performance, in percent correct from 0 to 100, against the number of IT recording sites on a logarithmic axis, 1, 4, 16, 64 and 256. The red curve, categorization (which of 8 categories), rises from near its chance level of about 12 percent to about 94 percent at 256 sites. The blue curve, identification (which of 77 pictures), rises from near zero to about 70 percent. Dotted horizontal lines mark the two chance levels. The point: a linear readout of a few hundred IT sites names the category reliably.
pub_hung2005_fig2.png: Hung, Kreiman, Poggio and DiCarlo (2005), Figure 2 top: six bars of classification performance, percent correct, with a dashed chance line near 12 percent. Below each bar, the TRAIN row shows the monkey face at the size and position used to train the readout: 3.4 degrees at the centre; 3.4 degrees at the centre; 1.7 degrees at the centre; 6.8 degrees at the centre; 3.4 degrees shifted 2 degrees; 3.4 degrees shifted 4 degrees. The TEST rows show the other sizes and positions it was tested on. The first bar, tested at the training size and position, is about 77 percent; the five bars tested on new sizes and positions are all near 70 percent. The point: a readout trained at one size and position still works at others.
pub_fukushima1980_fig2.png: Fukushima (1980), Figure 2: the Neocognitron's layers drawn left to right as stacks of planes, the input layer U0, then US1, UC1, US2, UC2, US3 and UC3. Each layer holds several cell planes, labelled k = 1 at the top to k = K at the bottom of each stack. Lines from a small circle in one plane to a cell in the next layer show that each cell reads a small patch of the layer before; the planes shrink and the patches cover more of the input with depth. In the last layer, UC3, each plane is a single cell. The point: alternating S (template) and C (pooling) layers build a cell that responds to a whole pattern wherever it sits.
pub_serre2007_wiring_hmax.png: Serre, Wolf, Bileschi, Riesenhuber and Poggio (2007), Figure 1, in three parts. Left: a wiring diagram of the macaque visual system, boxes for visual areas joined by arrows, split by a dashed line into the dorsal 'where' stream and the ventral 'what' stream, with V1, V2, V4, PIT and AIT highlighted in colour and prefrontal areas at the top. Middle: the model, rows of solid circles (simple units) and dashed circles (complex units) alternating from oriented filters on a photograph of cows, up through orange, green and blue units, to a purple 'animal vs. non-animal' unit; light blue lines are bypass routes. Right: a table of the model layers S1, C1, S2, C2, S2b, S3, C2b, C3 and S4, with receptive-field sizes growing from 0.2 to 1.1 degrees at S1 to 7 degrees at the top, and unit counts from 10 to the 7 down to 1 classification unit. The point: each stage of the model is matched to a stage of the ventral stream.
stride_padding.svg: Two panels showing how stride and padding set the size of a feature map. Left: a 5 by 5 input surrounded by one ring of zeros (padding 1), making a 7 by 7 grid. A 3 by 3 filter window, outlined in magenta, sits at the top-left; a dashed copy one column to the right is labelled stride 1. An arrow leads to the output, a 5 by 5 grid. Right: the same padded input, with the dashed window moved two columns, labelled stride 2; the output is 3 by 3. The point: a larger stride makes a smaller map, and padding lets the filter sit on the border.
pooling.svg: One 4 by 4 feature map whose rows read 0, 2, 1, 0; 3, 5, 0, 1; 0, 1, 4, 2; and 1, 0, 6, 0, shaded as four 2 by 2 windows. An upper arrow, labelled 'largest value in each window', leads to a 2 by 2 map reading 5, 1 on top and 1, 6 below: max-pooling with 2 by 2 windows and stride 2. A lower arrow, labelled 'average over all 16 positions', leads to a single value, 1.625: global average pooling, one number per map. The point: pooling turns a map into fewer numbers, keeping whether a feature is present rather than exactly where.
pub_serre2010_acm_table.png: Serre and Poggio (2010): a table of data that the HMAX model accounts for, with columns for brain area, type of data, and reference numbers for the biological and model data. Rows by area. Psychophysics: rapid animal categorization; face inversion effect. LOC: face processing (fMRI). PFC: differential role of IT and PFC in categorization. IT: tuning and invariance properties; read-out for object category; average effect in IT. V4: MAX operation; tuning for two-bar stimuli; two-spot interaction; tuning for boundary conformation; tuning for Cartesian and non-Cartesian gratings. V1: simple and complex cell tuning properties; MAX operation in a subset of complex cells. Text colour marks each row's status: black, data used to set the parameters; red, data the model agrees with; blue, predictions made before the data. The point: one model with one set of parameters was tested from V1 to behaviour.
hmax_vs_human_dprime.png: Serre, Oliva and Poggio (2007): performance on rapid animal versus non-animal categorization, measured as d-prime (d′, how well hits are separated from false alarms), from 1.0 to 2.6, at four viewing distances: head, close-body, medium-body and far-body. The model is a solid red line and human observers a blue dashed line, both with error bars. Both rise from head, about 2.2 for the model and 2.4 for people, to a peak near 2.5 at close-body, then fall to about 1.4 at far-body; the error bars overlap at every distance. The point: the feedforward model matches human accuracy across the four conditions.
hmax_stimuli.png: The stimulus set of Serre, Oliva and Poggio (2007): eight greyscale photographs in two rows under four column labels, head, close-body, medium-body and far-body. The top row shows animals at increasing distance: a leopard's head, a deer grazing, a small animal in a dark field, and distant animals in a landscape. The bottom row shows matched distractor scenes without animals at the same scales: a flower, a rocky stream, rock formations, and an open field. The point: the task is to say whether an animal is present, at four viewing distances.
residual_block.svg: A residual block drawn top to bottom. The block input, bold A, enters three stacked boxes: a 1 by 1 convolution with BatchNorm and ReLU, a 3 by 3 convolution with BatchNorm and ReLU, and a 1 by 1 convolution with BatchNorm. A magenta bracket labels the three boxes 'F of A: the change the block learns'. A green line, the skip connection, carries A unchanged around the boxes to a plus node, where it is added to F of A. A ReLU follows, and the block output is g of, A plus F of A. The point: the block learns only a change to its input, so the input can pass through when no change is needed.
resnet50_stages_f1.svg: ResNet-50 drawn left to right as a chain of squares joined by arrows, each labelled with its map size. A 224 by 224 photograph of a tiger (the image), then conv1, a 7 by 7 convolution at stride 2, 112 by 112; max-pool, 56 by 56; layer1, 3 blocks, 56 by 56; layer2, 4 blocks, 28 by 28; layer3, 6 blocks, 14 by 14; layer4, 3 blocks, 7 by 7; global average, 1 by 1; and a readout box. The four block groups are outlined in magenta and the squares shrink from left to right. The point: 16 residual blocks in four groups, each group after the first halving the maps' height and width.
batchnorm.svg: Three histograms stacked vertically, all on the same horizontal axis of activation value from minus 10 to 10, for one channel of ResNet-50's first layer over 64 Imagenette photographs and every position. Top, in blue, before normalization: mean minus 0.81, standard deviation 3.19, a sharp peak near zero with long tails out to about minus 10 and 10. Middle, in grey, after subtracting the batch mean and dividing by the batch standard deviation: mean 0.00, standard deviation 1.00. Bottom, in magenta, after the learned scale gamma and shift beta: mean 0.58, standard deviation 0.36, a narrow peak just above zero. A dashed line marks each mean. The point: BatchNorm standardizes each channel, then rescales it with learned values.
bn_modes.svg: A flow diagram in two rows. Top row, training mode, model.train(): a box 'a minibatch of images' leads to 'batch mean mu-B and variance sigma-B squared', then to 'normalize, then gamma and beta', then to the next layer. A blue arrow labelled 'updates' runs down from the batch statistics to a yellow box, 'stored running mean and variance'. Bottom row, evaluation mode, model.eval(): 'images to classify' leads straight to 'normalize, then gamma and beta' and the next layer, with a grey arrow labelled 'used' coming from the stored running mean and variance. The point: training normalizes with each minibatch's own statistics; evaluation uses the stored ones.
resnet50_stages_f2.svg: The same ResNet-50 chain as the earlier diagram, from a 224 by 224 tiger photograph through conv1, max-pool, layer1 to layer4, global average and readout, with the same map sizes. Now coloured by what is trained: conv1, max-pool and layer1 to layer3 are grey, labelled in the legend 'frozen: weights kept'; layer4 and the readout are solid magenta, 'trained on the new task (fine-tuned)'. The point: fine-tuning can keep the early block groups fixed and retrain only the last block group and the readout.
pub_krizhevsky2012_fig3.png: Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton (2012), Figure 3: AlexNet's 96 first-layer filters, each 11 by 11 by 3, shown as small colour tiles in six rows of sixteen. The top three rows are mostly grey-scale oriented edges and stripe patterns (gratings) at many orientations and widths. The bottom three rows are mostly colour blobs and colour edges, with a few checkerboard patterns and fine vertical stripes. The point: training on labelled images alone produced oriented, Gabor-like filters similar to V1 simple cells.
ringach_frame2_alexnet.svg: Scatter plot of receptive-field shape, each point placed by two numbers from a Gabor fit. Horizontal axis: n-x, the width in cycles of the grating, from 0 to 1.4. Vertical axis: n-y, the length in cycles, from 0 to 1.4. Filled grey squares are 93 macaque V1 simple cells (Ringach 2002); open green circles are the 32 AlexNet first-layer filters that a Gabor fits well. The cells run along a diagonal band from near the origin to about 0.8 wide and 1.4 long, densest below 0.5. The filters overlap the cells around 0.3 to 0.6 wide and 0.5 to 0.9 long, but several sit further right, up to 1.3 wide. The point: the network's filters resemble V1 cells, but tend to be wider, with more cycles.
template_matching_responses.png: Three AlexNet first-layer units, one per row. On the left of each row, outlined in magenta, the unit's weights shown as an 11 by 11 colour patch: oriented stripes in each case. To the right, the 9 natural image patches, out of 6,400, that drive the unit hardest, each with its response relative to the strongest patch. Unit 1, a dark diagonal stripe: 1.00, 0.91, 0.90, 0.87, 0.82, 0.77, 0.76, 0.73, 0.73. Unit 2, a blue and yellow oblique edge: 1.00, 0.83, 0.77, 0.70, 0.69, 0.68, 0.67, 0.67, 0.65. Unit 3, green and purple stripes: 1.00, 0.97, 0.92, 0.78, 0.68, 0.68, 0.64, 0.62, 0.61. For the striped units, the top patches show stripes at the same angle as the weights. The point: a first-layer unit acts as a template that the best-matching patches resemble.
hierarchy_meis_vs_physiology.png: A grid comparing ResNet-50 units with physiology. Four rows, labelled conv1, layer2, layer3 and layer4, each with six square panels. Conv1 shows the learned 7 by 7 filters as coarse colour patches: colour bars, blobs and small checks. Layer2, layer3 and layer4 show feature visualizations (images optimized to drive one unit; Fel et al. 2023): stripes and textures in layer2, repeated rounded patterns and object-part-like motifs in layer3, and dense clusters of object-like parts in layer4. A right-hand column, 'what electrophysiologists show each area', has three oriented gratings beside conv1 (V1: oriented bars, Hubel and Wiesel 1962), Pasupathy and Connor's curved silhouettes beside layer3 (V4, 2001), and Tanaka's table of critical features beside layer4 (IT, 1996); the layer2 row has no physiology panel. The pairings illustrate stimulus complexity, not a measured layer-to-area match. The point: complexity grows with depth in both.
cnn_era_timeline.png: ImageNet top-5 accuracy against year for five networks, drawn with the layer count beside each point: AlexNet 2012, 83.6 percent, 8 layers; ZFNet 2013, 88.3 percent, 8 layers; GoogLeNet 2014, 93.3 percent, 22 layers; VGG-16 2014, 92.7 percent, 16 layers; ResNet-152 2015, 96.4 percent, 152 layers, highlighted. Accuracy rises every year as depth grows.
pub_yamins2014_fig1a.png: Reproduced from Yamins et al. (2014), Figure 1A: a scatter of thousands of networks built from HMAX-like operations with different settings. Horizontal axis: categorization performance (balanced accuracy), from 0.5 to above 0.7. Vertical axis: the percentage of IT response variance the network's top layer predicts, from minus 15 to 30 percent. Three colours mark how the networks were chosen: orange, optimized to fit IT (correlation r = 0.80); blue, optimized for categorization performance (r = 0.78); green, random selection (r = 0.55). The blue cloud extends furthest up and to the right, reaching about 0.72 accuracy and 30 percent. The point: networks selected only for recognition also predict IT best.
Reproduced from Schrimpf et al. (2018), Figure 2: Brain-Score, from about 0.33 to 0.55, against ImageNet top-1 accuracy, from 0 to 80 percent, one dot per network. Grey dots, mostly small networks, run from accuracy near 0 with Brain-Scores of 0.32 to 0.38 up to about 45 percent and 0.50; labelled among them is 'best basenet'. Green dots are published deep networks, from 'alexnet' near 57 percent and 0.49 up to near 80 percent and 0.55; 'best mobilenet' is labelled, and a box encloses the top-right cluster. The annotation reads r = 0.92. The point: across these networks, ImageNet accuracy predicted the fit to brain data.
tics2026_neural_alignment.png: Linsley, Feng and Serre (2026): neural alignment, from 0 to 1.0 (how well a network's features predict monkey IT), against ImageNet multi-label accuracy, from about 0.45 to 1.0, for several hundred networks shown as coloured squares. Legend: CNN trained on ImageNet-1K, red; CNN on internet-scale vision, pink; adversarially trained CNN, yellow; convolutional vision transformers (ConvViT) on ImageNet-1K, dark green, and internet-scale, light green; vision transformers (ViT) on ImageNet-1K, blue, internet-scale vision, light blue, and internet-scale vision and language, grey. A grey vertical band near 0.92 to 0.97 marks human accuracy. One dashed line rises from about 0.48 alignment at the left to about 0.68 near 0.92 accuracy; a second dashed line falls from there to the right. Purple stars mark recent models: SigLIP-2 and DINOv3 ViT-L near 0.63 to 0.65, I-JEPA near 0.49, DINOv3 ViT-H near 0.55, EVA-02 near 0.98 accuracy and 0.47, and vJEPA2 lowest at about 0.29. The point: alignment rises with accuracy up to about human accuracy, then falls.
geirhos_cue_conflict.png: Three images from Geirhos et al. (2019) with labels underneath. Left, 'Shape: cat': a photograph of a ginger cat lying down on a white background. Middle, 'Texture: elephant': a close-up of grey, wrinkled elephant skin. Right, 'Cue conflict': the cat's outline filled with the elephant-skin texture, so the shape says cat and the texture says elephant. The point: such images separate what a network relies on, shape or texture.
pub_zeiler2014_fig7ad_row.png: Zeiler and Fergus (2014), Figure 7, three pairs side by side. Each pair is a test photograph with a grey square drawn on it, and to its right a map of the probability of the correct class as the square is moved over every position: red is high, blue is low. Pair 1, true label Pomeranian: a fluffy dog holding a green toy; the map is red everywhere except a blue patch where the square covers the dog's face. Pair 2, true label car wheel: the side of a racing car; the map is blue over the wheel on the right. Pair 3, true label Afghan hound: a man and a woman with a long-haired dog; the map is blue over the dog and red over the man's face. The point: covering the object, not its surroundings, lowers the network's probability.
flower_three_methods.png: Four square panels left to right, computed for the next assignment's flower network (ResNet-50 with a linear readout for 102 flower species) on one test photograph, a magenta petunia that the network calls morning glory with probability 0.63. Panel 1, photograph: a five-lobed magenta flower with a dark centre, green leaves around it. Panel 2, saliency (gradient): bright orange and yellow speckles spread over the whole flower, a little denser near the centre. Panel 3, Grad-CAM (layer4): one smooth bright blob over the dark centre, fading outward. Panel 4, occlusion (grey square): a coarse blocky map whose brightest blocks are also on the centre. All three maps are for the class morning glory, brighter meaning more important. The point: three methods give three different-looking maps of one decision.
flower_gradcam_two_classes.png: Three square panels. Left, the photograph: the magenta petunia with a dark centre. Middle, Grad-CAM for morning glory, the network's answer, p = 0.633: a smooth bright blob centred on the flower's dark centre. Right, Grad-CAM for petunia, the true class, p = 0.000: a bright spot on the same centre and a second bright patch in the bottom-right corner, outside the flower. Each map is scaled to its own peak, so both look equally bright. The point: a map can be made for any class, even one the network gives almost zero probability.
flower_intervention.png: Four panels testing the Grad-CAM map. Panel 1, Grad-CAM for morning glory, with the brightest region, the flower's dark centre, outlined in blue. Panel 2, map region inpainted: the same photograph with that outlined region filled in from its surroundings, so the centre becomes smooth magenta petal. Panel 3, control, same shape: the same outline inpainted on a petal near the top, the centre left intact. Panel 4, a dot plot of the probability of morning glory, from 0 to 1.0: one blue dot at 0.00 for the map's region, and 30 grey dots for random same-shape controls spread between 0.30 and 0.93, around a dotted line marking the original 0.63. The point: removing the region the map highlights removes the decision; removing an equal area elsewhere does not.
flower_deletion_curves.svg: Left, the petunia photograph, labelled true: petunia, predicted: morning glory, p = 0.633. Right, deletion curves: probability of morning glory, from 0 to 1.0, against the fraction of pixels removed, from 0 to 1.0 in steps of 0.1, pixels replaced by a blurred copy in the order each map ranks them. All curves start at 0.63. Occlusion, red, drops to near 0 by 0.1, area under the curve 0.04. Grad-CAM, green, drops to about 0.1 and stays low, area 0.08. Saliency, blue, area 0.18, and integrated gradients, magenta, area 0.21, fall more slowly with bumps. The random map, dashed grey, stays between 0.6 and 0.8 until about 0.7, area 0.58. The point: a good map falls fast; occlusion and Grad-CAM beat the random map by far.
pub_adebayo2018_fig2_rows.png: Reproduced from Adebayo et al. (2018), Figure 2: the cascading randomization test on an Inception v3 network. Top left, the original image: a grey and white bird (a junco) on a branch. Columns, left to right: the original explanation, then the network with its layers randomized one after another from the top (logits, mixed_7c, mixed_7b and so on) down to the bottom (conv2d_1a_3x3). Rows: Gradient, Guided Back-propagation, GradCAM, Guided GradCAM and Integrated Gradients. The Gradient row loses the bird's faint outline gradually as more layers are randomized. The GradCAM row is a single red blob in the original and changes to blocky patterns as soon as the top layers are randomized. The two Guided rows keep a clear outline of the bird in nearly every column. The Integrated Gradients row keeps a faint bird outline throughout. The point: a map that survives random weights does not reflect what the network learned.
gradcam_cue_conflict.png: Three square panels, computed with an ImageNet ResNet-50 on a cue-conflict image from Geirhos et al. (2019). Left, 'cat shape, elephant texture': a cat's outline filled with grey, wrinkled elephant skin. Middle, Grad-CAM for 'African elephant', p = 0.64: a broad bright yellow region over most of the cat's body. Right, Grad-CAM for 'tabby', p below 0.001: the image darkened, with one bright spot at the top edge and a fainter one in the top-right corner. The point: the elephant map covers the cat's body, but cannot say whether the shape or the skin texture at those pixels drove the decision.
shortcut_toy.png: Our replication of Geirhos et al. (2020), Figure 2. Four square images, each divided into quarters, then a bar chart. Image 1, training, star: a black star in the bottom-left quarter. Image 2, training, moon: a black crescent moon in the top-left quarter. Image 3, in red, new place, star: a star in the bottom-right quarter, which the network calls moon. Image 4, new place, moon: a moon in the bottom-left quarter, which the network calls star. Bar chart: accuracy, from 0 to 1.0; green bar, same layout as training, 1.00; red bar, shapes moved, 0.50, on a dotted line marking chance. The point: the network learned the position of the shape, not the shape.
same_accuracy.svg: Ten numbered photographs in two rows, each with its true label and the predictions of two classifiers, A and B, marked correct or error. Top row, all true label wolf: 1, a wolf among snowy trees; 2, a wolf walking on snow; 3, a wolf on snowy rocks; 4, a wolf sitting in snow; 5, a wolf on green grass. Bottom row, all true label husky: 6, a red husky standing on snow; 7, a grey husky by a wooden wall with snow behind; 8, 9 and 10, huskies on green grass. A errs on 1, 2 and 4, calling those wolves husky. B errs on 5, calling the wolf on grass husky, and on 6 and 7, calling the huskies in snow wolf. Both get 7 of 10 correct. A caption asks which image cue explains B's errors. The predictions are illustrative. The point: equal accuracy can hide different strategies.
featvis_hierarchy_4rows.png: A grid computed for the course with MACO (Fel et al. 2023). Four rows of networks: AlexNet, ResNet-50, ViT-B/16 and DINOv2 ViT-B/14. Three column groups of four units each: low layer, middle layer and high layer. The low column shows first-layer filters, not optimized images: oriented stripes and colour blobs for AlexNet and ResNet-50, noisy multicoloured patches for the two vision transformers. The middle and high columns show feature visualizations, images optimized to drive one unit, each a round patch fading at the edge. Middle layer: repeated textures and small curved motifs such as scales and dots. High layer: dense clusters of object-like parts, such as eyes and spiky shapes. The point: edges, then textures, then object parts, across the depth of every network.
topk_resnet50_layer4.png: Three ResNet-50 layer4 units, one per row. In each row, the unit's MACO feature visualization on the left, labelled with its number, then the six ImageNet validation images that drive it most strongly. Unit 43: a bronze helmet, a triceratops skull, a thatched roof, a burrito, a thatched cottage, and two axes on grass. Unit 179: a bell, small metal screws, a perforated bone, a bolt and a screw, a birdhouse, and a shark. Unit 309: piled sleeping bags, a volcano above a town, a volcano over a lake, a volcano in cloud, a tent below snowy peaks, and a yurt. The point: unit 309 responds to conical shapes, while unit 179 has no single label.
camera_rotation.png: Bau, Zhou, Khosla, Oliva and Torralba (2017): number of unique concept detectors among one AlexNet layer's units, from 0 to 40, as the layer's representation is rotated, at baseline (no rotation) and rotations of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1. Six dashed lines, one per concept type. Object, blue: 36, 36, 33, 27, 10, 6. Texture, green: 20, 21, 20, 17, 8, 5. Scene, yellow: 12, 13, 13, 9, 1, 2. Part, orange: 8, 8, 8, 8, 4, 2. Colour, light blue: about 2 falling to 0. Material, purple: about 1 throughout. The point: rotating the layer leaves distances between images unchanged, yet most of the detectors disappear.
13_more_features_than_dims.svg: Two circles, each drawn around arrows from its centre. Left, titled '2 features, one per unit': two blue arrows at right angles, one pointing right and one pointing up, captioned 'perpendicular: each unit means one thing'. Right, titled '7 features in the same 2 units': seven magenta arrows spread around the circle, captioned 'they must overlap, so each unit means several'. The point: when there are more features than units, features become directions that mix several units, so a single unit responds to several unrelated things.
flower_four_methods.png: Five panels in a row, each 224 by 224 pixels. First, the petunia photograph: a pink flower with a dark centre, a second flower in the lower right corner. Then four attribution maps for the class morning glory drawn in the inferno colour scale over a greyed copy of the photograph, each scaled to its own 99.5th percentile. Saliency: fine bright speckle spread over the whole flower. Integrated gradients: credit concentrated on the dark centre and along the petal veins and edges, with less speckle. Grad-CAM: one smooth bright blob on the dark centre. Occlusion: a coarse grid of 32-pixel squares, brightest on the centre. The maps agree on the centre and differ in how fine they are.
flower_ig_only.png: Two panels. Left, the petunia photograph. Right, its integrated-gradients map for the class morning glory, computed with a blurred copy of the photograph as the baseline: bright credit on the flower's dark centre and along the petal veins and edges, much less speckle than the saliency map, and almost nothing on the background.
pub_hw_ganglion_simple_complex.png: Three columns of icons summarizing Hubel and Wiesel's V1: on the left an on-centre and an off-centre circle for retinal and LGN cells; in the middle an oriented bar at one position for a simple cell; on the right an oriented bar with arrows showing it can sit anywhere in the field, for a complex cell. The point: a weighted sum builds selectivity, a pooling builds tolerance.
pooling_frame0.svg: Computed on model cells. Left: five identical simple cells in a row with overlapping oriented receptive fields, a bar of light outside all of them, no spikes, all five converging on one complex cell below. Right: response against the bar's position, with nothing drawn yet. The complex cell is silent because no simple cell is driven.
pooling_frame3.svg: Computed on model cells. Left: the bar sits on the third simple cell's field; that cell fires most and the complex cell fires. Right: response against the bar's position: the first three of five simple-cell bumps are drawn, and the complex cell's broad curve, their sum, stays high across them.
pooling_frame6.svg: Computed on model cells. Left: the bar has passed all five fields. Right: five overlapping bumps, one per simple cell, each covering a narrow range of positions, and the complex cell's broad curve covering all five with small dips between them: tolerance to position, with the orientation preference of its inputs.
conv_frame1.png: The tiger photograph in grey levels, 224 by 224, an arrow to one 11 by 11 vertical Gabor filter, an arrow to the feature map, 224 by 224, bright where the image has vertical stripes. One set of weights is reused at every position, so shifting the image shifts the map.
s12_img00_noletters.png: DiCarlo, Zoccolan and Rust 2012, Figure 1: a side view of the macaque brain with the ventral visual stream drawn from the eye through LGN, V1, V2, V4 to the inferior temporal cortex, and beside it the same areas stacked as boxes, each with its typical response latency, rising from about 40 milliseconds in V1 to about 100 milliseconds in IT, and an approximate neuron count per stage.
pub_felleman1991_hierarchy.png: Felleman and Van Essen's 1991 diagram of the macaque visual system: 32 cortical areas drawn as coloured boxes arranged in about ten levels, from the retina and LGN at the bottom, through V1, V2, V3, V4 and MT in the middle, to the inferotemporal and frontal areas at the top, connected by hundreds of lines. The ordering follows the layers each connection starts and ends in; the ventral stream is one path through it.
pub_kobatake_tanaka1994_critical_feature: Kobatake and Tanaka's 1994 table of critical features by cortical area, four columns. V2: a triangle and a bullseye. V4: a star, a circle with a dot, a textured bar, a cross, a dark square with a corner, concentric rings. Posterior IT: a leaf shape, a cross, concentric rings, a star, a half disc, a dotted bar, a striped half circle. Anterior IT: a striped block, a dark blob, concentric rings, a cartoon face, a square with a dark bar, a circle on a stem, a flask shape, a blob, a striped bar with a ball. Preferred stimuli grow from simple patterns to object parts and faces.
pub_pasupathy2001_shapes.png: The 51 simple closed shapes used by Pasupathy and Connor in 2001, drawn as black silhouettes in six rows: a dot and a disc, ovals, crescents, teardrops, three-lobed and four-lobed shapes, and rounded forms with one sharp point. One shape in the second row is outlined in red as the example used on the next panel.
pub_pasupathy2001_curvature_angle.png: One of the shapes, a black form with two sharp convex points, drawn with grey axes through its centre and red circles marking points on its boundary at angular positions 0, 45, 90, 135, 225, 270 and 315 degrees. A V4 cell's response is described by the curvature of the boundary at one such angular position.
gallant_gratings.png: Nine circular grating patches in three rows, drawn from the stimulus formulas. Cartesian: parallel stripes at three orientations. Polar: concentric rings, radial spokes, and a spiral. Hyperbolic: saddle-shaped patterns at three rotations. Gallant and colleagues found V4 cells that prefer the polar or hyperbolic patterns to any stripes.
pub_freeman2013_textures.png: Freeman and colleagues 2013, Figure 1, panels a to c. Panel a: three photographs of textures, honeycomb, grains and a mesh. Panel b: each turned into noise that matches only the responses of V1-like oriented filters, labelled spectrally matched noise; the noise looks blotchy. Panel c: textures that also match the correlations between the filters, labelled naturalistic texture; these look like the originals. V2 cells, unlike V1 cells, respond more to panel c than to panel b.
hmax_scale_bands.png: A four by four grid of Gabor filters as grey images: columns for orientations 0, 45, 90 and 135 degrees, rows for sizes 7, 11, 15 and 19 pixels, the stripes getting coarser down the rows. Magenta boxes group each orientation's two adjacent sizes: the pairs a C1 unit takes the maximum over, in addition to the maximum over nearby positions.
hmax_ventral_hierarchy.png: HMAX drawn beside the ventral stream: S1 and C1 units over V1 and V2, S2 and C2 units over V4, S3 units over IT and a readout over prefrontal cortex. Each S stage is a weighted sum over the C stage below, each C stage a maximum over the S stage below, and the receptive fields widen at every step up.
vgg_stack.svg: Two diagrams. Left: a single 7 by 7 grid of weights, labelled one 7 by 7 filter: it sees 7 by 7 pixels, 49 weights, one ReLU. Right: three nested grids of 3, 5 and 7 cells, labelled three 3 by 3 filters in a row: the receptive field grows from 3 to 5 to 7 pixels with 27 weights and three ReLUs.
demo_occlusion.png: A still of the occlusion demo: an ImageNet photograph of an English springer spaniel on a lawn with a hen, a 32-pixel grey square over the hen's head; beside it five bars giving ResNet-50's probability for English springer, hen and three other dog classes, each with a tick at its value on the clean photograph; and the swept occlusion map for the class hen, bright over the hen and dark over the dog.
hmax_ventral_hierarchy_cream.png: HMAX drawn beside the ventral stream: S1 and C1 units over V1 and V2, S2 and C2 units over V4, S3 units over IT and a readout over prefrontal cortex. Each S stage is a weighted sum over the C stage below, each C stage a maximum over the S stage below, and the receptive fields widen at every step up.
pub_dicarlo2012_fig1b_boxes.png: DiCarlo, Zoccolan and Rust 2012, Figure 1, right panel: the ventral-stream areas drawn as stacked boxes, retina and LGN at the bottom, then V1, V2, V4, posterior, central and anterior IT, with arrows up between them. Beside each stage its typical response latency, about 40 milliseconds at the LGN, 50 in V1, 60 in V2, 70 in V4, 80 to 100 in IT, and an approximate neuron count, from about one million to tens of millions.
pub_bau2017_camera_rotation_cream.png: Bau, Zhou, Khosla, Oliva and Torralba (2017): number of unique concept detectors among one AlexNet layer's units, from 0 to 40, as the layer's representation is rotated, at baseline (no rotation) and rotations of 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 and 1. Six dashed lines, one per concept type. Object, blue: 36, 36, 33, 27, 10, 6. Texture, green: 20, 21, 20, 17, 8, 5. Scene, yellow: 12, 13, 13, 9, 1, 2. Part, orange: 8, 8, 8, 8, 4, 2. Colour, light blue: about 2 falling to 0. Material, purple: about 1 throughout. The point: rotating the layer leaves distances between images unchanged, yet most of the detectors disappear.
flower_saliency_pair.png: Two panels: the petunia photograph, and its saliency map for the class morning glory drawn over a darkened copy of the photograph, a speckle of bright pixels spread over the whole flower and densest at the dark centre.
flower_gradcam_pair.png: Two panels: the petunia photograph, and its Grad-CAM map for the class morning glory, one smooth bright blob centred on the flower's dark centre and fading over the petals.
